India pacers Arshdeep Singh , Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi will remain with the team for preparations ahead of the Test series against New Zealand, batting coach Sitanshu Kotak confirmed on Saturday.The three pacers will stay back after the ODI series as the team begins its preparations for the red-ball challenge.Speaking at the press conference ahead of the third ODI, Kotak said the conditions in the ongoing ODI series had provided useful preparation for the Test matches, particularly for the bowling unit."Both pitches had seam and swing. Good preparations for the Test because the ball will change, but one-day cricket does give you an idea about the conditions. The thickness of the grass and everything. It's been challenging but good for the team and preparations," Kotak said.He also pointed to the three India A matches as an important part of the build-up, saying they had ensured adequate preparation for both batters and bowlers.India's Test players are scheduled to begin a preparatory camp on November 11. Kotak expects the sessions to help the squad get ready for the series."India Test players will start their camp from the 11th, so hopefully those five-six sessions will help get prepared for the Test series," he said.Providing details of the team's immediate plans, Kotak confirmed that head coach Gautam Gambhir would remain with the ODI squad, while he and bowling coach Morne Morkel would travel to Wellington."Gurnoor, Arshdeep and Nabi will stay back for Test preparations. Gambhir stays back with the ODI team, me and Morne will go to Wellington. That's the plan for now," he said.Kotak also spoke about KL Rahul's importance to the Indian batting line-up, praising his adaptability and ability to deliver according to the team's requirements.Rahul remained unbeaten on 26 during India's rain-affected chase of 135 in the second ODI. With wickets falling at regular intervals, the wicketkeeper-batter held one end together as India reached 113/7 in 26 overs before rain brought the contest to an end."Biggest advantage is he opens in Test cricket. He is someone who plays according to the need of the team. Since I have joined, he has played unbelievable innings. Never looks under pressure and has never let the team down. Can rotate and can easily hit sixes," Kotak said.On India's approach to playing additional all-rounders, the batting coach said team selection was based on players performing their designated roles rather than making compromises to accommodate an extra batter."We are playing players at the spot. Difficult to reduce a bowler and add a batter," he explained.Meanwhile, India moved 2-0 ahead in the five-match ODI series after edging New Zealand by four runs under the DLS method in Wellington.Defending a modest target of 135 in a contest reduced to 47 overs per side, New Zealand had India in trouble at 113/7 after 26 overs when rain forced the players off the field. India were four runs ahead of the DLS par score, handing them victory.Gurnoor Brar was the standout performer with the ball, claiming 4/30 in 10 overs, while Auqib Nabi picked up two wickets. Anshul Kamboj and Axar Patel also finished with two wickets apiece.Earlier, Daryl Mitchell top-scored for New Zealand with 55, rescuing the hosts from 53/5 through a 59-run partnership with Mitchell Santner, who contributed 31.India will now head to Hamilton for the third ODI on Tuesday, looking to extend their advantage in the series.

Article Title: Kansas City Chiefs could make a season-changing trade before the 2026 NFL deadline, but there's a catch
Article Text:
Kansas City Chiefs Have a Big Trade Deadline Call to Make (Getty Images)

Chiefs could trade for a wide receiver before the 2026 NFL deadline

Chris Godwin and Brian Thomas lead the list of possible targets

Deadline rules and the trades already made

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Kansas City Chiefs have until 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, to make a trade, and the clock is short. Kansas City has lost two straight road games, to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos. Against Denver, the Chiefs had a chance to win on the final play, but a false start made the red-zone attempt harder. Patrick Mahomes needs more help, and several wide receivers have been linked to the team. Here is where the market stands.Wide receiver is the clearest hole on the roster. ESPN’s Nate Taylor named a receiver as the Chiefs’ top priority before the deadline, and the numbers back him up. Travis Kelce , a tight end, leads the team with 29 catches for 410 yards and two touchdowns. Xavier Worthy is second with 27 catches, but he has just 230 yards and one score. Rashee Rice has 243 receiving yards. Running back Emmett Johnson has 237, and 70 of those came on one play. Tyquan Thornton gave the offense another option until an injury took him out.Kenneth Walker III, signed in the offseason, has helped the backfield. That solved one problem. The passing game still looks thin for a team built around Mahomes.Several receivers have been tied to Kansas City, though none looks like a sure thing.Seth Walder pointed to Tampa Bay’s Chris Godwin. He has played his whole NFL career with the Buccaneers and would give Mahomes an experienced target. Jacksonville’s Brian Thomas is the younger name. The Jaguars would have to agree to move him, and nothing says they will.Former quarterback Russell Wilson floated New York Jets receiver Garrett Wilson. The reports supplied do not say whether the Jets would listen. Tyreek Hill has come up too, but he is not expected to play until at least December, which limits what he could add down the stretch.Kansas City has not announced a deal for any of them.The deadline falls after Week 9 for the third straight season. The league once held it after Week 6, then moved it to the Tuesday after Week 8 in 2012. Owners pushed it back one more week in 2024. After 4 p.m. ET (3 p.m. CT) Tuesday, no trades can be completed until the offseason. The Chiefs can still sign free agents.Other teams have not waited. According to USA TODAY Sports, the Giants got quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings on September 28 for a fifth-round pick. Dallas added cornerback Joey Porter Jr. from Pittsburgh on October 1. Baltimore landed lineman Cam Jurgens from Philadelphia on October 7, and Houston picked up Marvin Harrison Jr.from Arizona on October 12.Late October brought more. Seattle acquired Quenton Nelson from Indianapolis on October 27. The Colts sent DeForest Buckner to San Francisco a day later. Chicago got Jeffery Simmons from Tennessee on October 29. Then on November 4, Baltimore added quarterback Jacoby Brissett from the Cardinals.Kansas City has two days left to join them.

Article Title: In 2020, Cooper Kupp paid $2.5 million sight unseen for a 4-acre Wilsonville, Oregon home; he added a 4,600 sq ft indoor training hall and sold it in 2024 for $3 million
Article Text:
Image of Cooper Kupp, a wide receiver with the Los Angeles Rams. (Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons)

A pandemic project turned a barn into a football training facility

Representative image of American football players practising agility drills. (Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons)

The house, its grounds, and the final sale

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An offseason for a professional athlete could be a luxury home they can retreat to, and that would not be unusual. But what’s unheard of is if it were also a training ground. Cooper Kupp, Los Angeles Rams wide receiver, brought this idea to life. In 2020, he bought a four-acre property in Wilsonville, Oregon, sight unseen, according to Realtor. By August 2024, it found new owners for $3 million, after $500,000 was trimmed from the asking price. Kupp had initially listed the four-acre estate in September 2023 for $3.5 million, per Robb Report.The sale brought one particular feature of the estate to the fore: a 4,600-square-foot indoor athletic facility, built inside what used to be a barn. Kupp had used the space during the off-season before the Rams won Super Bowl LVI. The property also included a main residence, accommodating five bedrooms, and a separate guest house. This gave the listing a mix of family accommodation and sporting space. Kupp’s decision to let go of the estate was tied to practicalities of family life. In its September 25, 2023 report, Robb Report said he and his wife had less time to travel to Oregon with their three children.The home was about 30 minutes from Portland. By the time the sale was reported in August 2024, the property had been on the market for 11 months.Because it was a celebrity home, its interior facilities were a major selling point. Robb Report described a turf-lined field, retractable basketball hoops at both ends, lighting, speakers and two oversized bay doors. In his own words, Kupp recalled the work that went into building and described it as a special part of the property. He said to the newspaper: “So much blood, sweat and tears went in there.”Kupp had fitted out the 4,600 square feet space during the pandemic. He also told Forber in 2023 that he completed most of his off-season preparations there before the Rams’ Super Bowl season. He added that the family had taken care in equipping the barn as a performance space center and that he would miss the early morning sessions done there. The facility was not the only space set aside designated for exercise. The four-car garage had been arranged as a gym. The indoor field room was used for football drills, and the retractable hoops were used for basketball practice.According to the Realtor, the main house was built in 1997. The rooms included an office with a fireplace, a family room with a bar and wine fridge, and a formal dining room with coffered ceilings and chandeliers. Robb Report added that the exterior design was Gothic Revival, with hardwood floors, natural stone details, large windows and decorative woodwork, natural stone details, large windows and decorative woodwork.The main residence had five bedrooms and 6.5 bathrooms. The kitchen had a large island and appliances by Miele and Sub-Zero, and later the former received updated appliances and hardware, along with paint, wallpaper, and stone finishes.The main bedroom had access to the rear grounds and an adjoining bathroom with a deep bath and glass shower. On the ground floor, the primary suite also had a private vestibule and its own patio. Upstairs, there were also four other bedrooms. The property also had a separate guest cottage. It included a bedroom, laundry room and covered patio. The estate sat on a little over four acres, about 17 miles south of Portland. Robb Report in 2023 had earlier described an almost 2,000-square-foot guest house.Kupp, who hails from Washington, played college football at Eastern Washington University before being selected by the Rams in the third round of the 2017 NFL Draft. He was named the Most Valuable Player of Super Bowl LVI, which the Rams won after the 2021 season.
Article Summary: Cooper Kupp, a wide receiver with the Los Angeles Rams, bought a four-acre property in Wilsonville, Oregon, sight unseen in 2020. By August 2024, it found new owners for $3 million, after $500,000 was trimmed from the asking price. The sale brought one particular feature of the estate to the fore: a 4,600-square- foot indoor athletic facility built inside what used to be a barn.

Article Title: In 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at 41,000 feet because fuel was calculated in pounds instead of kilograms; the pilots glided it onto a disused air base runway in Gimli, and all 69 on
Article Text:
Confusion over kilograms and pounds

Total power loss in mid-air

Race track diversion at Gimli

Landing on the dragstrip

An Air Canada Boeing 767 carrying 61 passengers and eight crew members ran completely out of fuel at 41,000 feet over Manitoba after a mistake in converting metric measurements caused ground staff to put less than half the required fuel into the aircraft. The pilots managed to glide the 132-tonne plane for 17 minutes without engine power. They made an emergency landing on a former military runway that had been turned into a sports car race track. According to the official inquiry by the Aviation Safety Board of Canada, all 69 people on board survived the incident on 23 July 1983. Only minor injuries were reported during the evacuation.The fueling mistake happened on the ground in Montreal before the flight departed for Edmonton via Ottawa. The aircraft's digital Fuel Quantity Indicator System (FQIS) was not working because of a faulty channel. Maintenance workers had already recorded the problem. Since the automatic fuel gauge showed no readings, the ground crew and pilots had to work out the fuel amount manually. They used a dripstick, a tool that measured the volume of fuel in litres. At the time, Air Canada was changing its fleet over to the metric system.The newly purchased Boeing 767 was the airline's first aircraft that used metric measurements throughout. The standard flight management computers required fuel amounts to be entered in kilograms. However, while doing the manual calculations, the crew used the conversion figure for pounds instead of kilograms. Instead of multiplying the fuel volume in litres by 0.8 to calculate its weight in kilograms, they multiplied it by 1.77. This was the conversion figure used for imperial measurements. Because of this mistake, the aircraft took off with just 22,300 pounds (10,100 kg) of fuel. This was only about 45 percent of the 49,200 pounds (22,300 kg) needed to complete the journey to Edmonton.While flying over Red Lake, Ontario, at 41,000 feet, the pilots received warnings about low fuel pressure in the cockpit. Captain Robert Pearson and First Officer Maurice Quintal first thought there was a problem with a fuel pump. They planned to divert the aircraft to Winnipeg. Within minutes, both Pratt & Whitney JT9D engines stopped working, cutting off power to all the main electrical generators. With both engines out, the cockpit displays went blank. The pilots were left with only a few emergency instruments powered by batteries. These backup instruments did not include a vertical speed indicator, which made it difficult for the crew to work out how quickly the aircraft was losing height. There was another serious problem. Without engine power to run the hydraulic pumps, the aircraft's control surfaces could no longer be moved using the normal controls. The aircraft's automatic emergency system released a ram air turbine. This was a small propeller powered by the airflow outside the aircraft. It produced just enough hydraulic pressure to let the pilots steer the plane and control its nose position manually.After realising they could not reach Winnipeg, First Officer Quintal suggested landing at the former Royal Canadian Air Force Station Gimli. This was a military airfield where he had trained in the past. The crew did not know that the closed military base had been turned into Gimli Motorsports Park. On the day of the incident, part of the main runway was being used for a sports car event organised by the Winnipeg Sports Car Club. Spectators, campers, and racing cars were parked along the runway. As Captain Pearson, who had years of experience as a glider pilot, brought the aircraft toward Gimli, he realised it was moving too fast and was too high to stop safely on the remaining paved runway. Since both engines had stopped, the crew could not use the wing flaps or slats to slow the aircraft down. Pearson used a forward slip, a rare move for commercial aircraft. It involves using the rudder and aileron controls in opposite directions to turn the aircraft sideways. This increases air resistance and helps the plane lose height quickly without increasing its forward speed. The sideways movement briefly reduced the airflow to the ram air turbine. This made the flight controls harder to operate just before landing. However, Pearson managed to straighten the aircraft in time.The crew lowered the landing gear using a manual gravity release system. The main landing gear locked into position, but the nose gear did not lock properly. The Boeing 767 touched down on the dragstrip section of the airfield. Pearson applied the main wheel brakes, causing two tyres to burst. Two boys riding bicycles on the runway managed to get out of the way as the silent aircraft approached them. Because the nose gear had not locked into place, the front of the aircraft dropped onto the runway. The nose scraped along the concrete, creating a great deal of friction that helped slow down the heavy plane. The front section then hit a steel guardrail installed along the middle of the converted dragstrip. The barrier helped keep the aircraft moving straight along the runway instead of turning toward the spectators. The aircraft came to a complete stop within 3,000 feet of touching down. A small fire near the nose was put out by race track staff using portable fire extinguishers. Passengers left the aircraft using emergency slides. Because the nose had collapsed, the slides hung at steep angles. Some passengers suffered minor cuts, scrapes, and sprains during the evacuation. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board report identified failures in procedures, gaps in staff training, and Air Canada's use of both metric and imperial measurements across its aircraft fleet as main factors behind the incident. The damaged Boeing 767, registered as C-GAUN, was repaired at the Gimli site and returned to commercial service with Air Canada. It continued flying for another 25 years before being retired in 2008.
Article Summary: All 69 people on board survived the incident on 23 July 1983. The fueling mistake happened on the ground in Montreal before the flight departed for Edmonton. The pilots managed to glide the 132-tonne plane for 17 minutes without engine power. They made an emergency landing on a former military runway that had been turned into a sports car race track.

Article Title: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian says he wants his daughter to use AI every day; reveals how she changed his understanding of the technology
Article Text:
Alexis Ohanian wants his daughter to explore big questions with AI

Alexis Ohanian says his daughter changed how he thinks about speaking to AI

AI is becoming part of her drawing sessions

Alexis Ohanian's vision for raising a daughter who can use AI as a creative superpower

Parenthood has influenced the way he thinks about technology

Alexis Ohanian has spent much of his career building and investing in technology, but one of his most useful lessons about artificial intelligence has come from watching his seven-year-old daughter use it. The Reddit co-founder says he wants Olympia to work with AI every day, treating it as a tool for asking questions, exploring ideas and developing her creativity. Their conversations at the dinner table have become part of that routine. Yet it is not simply what she asks about an AI system that has caught his attention. Watching her speak naturally to the technology has also made him reconsider assumptions he had carried from years of using computers.During an interview on the Possible podcast, hosted by Reid Hoffman and Aria Finger, Ohanian described a family routine built around asking a big question over dinner. It began before AI became part of the household. When his daughter was younger, he would try to answer her questions himself, looking things up when he did not know enough.“Even just seeing my own seven-year-old’s relationship to AI—and the ChatGPT app is definitely the one that runs all the numbers for us—and seeing the way she converses with it.Seeing the way we do a big question every night at dinner. And we started doing this pre-AI, and so poor papa had to be the answer, and we’d look it up if I didn’t know, but she was also younger, so the questions were a lot easier back then. But now the questions are getting harder. ”He sees this as a change in the way children can approach information. Previous generations had reference books and dictionaries, followed by search engines such as Google. For Olympia, conversational AI is becoming another way to find answers, but one that allows her to continue asking questions rather than stopping at a list of search results.Ohanian said he wants her to use the technology every day. His aim is not to make AI a replacement for learning, but to let her become comfortable using it while she develops her own interests and abilities.One of the more personal observations Ohanian shared concerned the way Olympia communicates with ChatGPT. He had spent years getting used to typing questions into computers and had little reason to reconsider that habit. His daughter approached the technology differently.For a child who has grown up with much better speech-recognition tools, speaking to an AI assistant can feel more natural than typing. Ohanian said watching her converse with the system helped him recognise that his own preference for typing was shaped by older experiences with speech-to-text software, which had often been unreliable.He recalled, “I think because I was so hung up with speech-to-text being bad for so much of my life, that it took a seven-year-old—who’s really only known amazing speech-to-text—to help me realize like, “My God, you’re right. This paradigm is here.” And this is the fun part.”Ohanian also described how he and Olympia have been experimenting with AI as part of their creative activities. He recently found some of his childhood sketchbooks, which his parents had kept, and photographed several of the drawings. Using a recent version of ChatGPT, he showed his daughter how those pencil sketches could be turned into coloured illustrations.Some of the drawings were unfinished. That did not prevent them from being transformed into more complete images, giving Olympia a chance to see how an early idea could develop into something different.The process has also become part of their drawing sessions. Ohanian said they follow tutorials from the YouTube channel Art for Kids, drawing alongside the instructor with physical markers and paper. Once they have finished, he can photograph their work and use AI tools to alter or extend the images. They can see a drawing brought to life, including imagined versions of it moving through space.For Ohanian, the technology adds possibilities to an existing activity rather than taking its place. The child remains involved in the creative work, while the software provides a way to see the result differently.Ohanian's enthusiasm for AI does not mean he wants his daughter to skip traditional learning. He specifically said that reading, writing and arithmetic remain fundamentals she needs to understand.He has also introduced Olympia to Synthesis Tutor to support her maths homework. He described it as part of the family's efforts to use available tools to help with learning, rather than relying on AI for every task.His wider point is that children will need to know how to make use of increasingly capable systems. He described AI as a kind of superpower that he wants Olympia to have, particularly when it comes to creativity and turning ideas into something tangible.In the interview, he suggested that the value of these tools would increasingly depend on what people chose to do with them. He spoke about agency, persistence and creativity as qualities that would remain important even as AI systems became more capable.Ohanian's comments about Olympia fit into a wider discussion about how technology should affect people's lives. He has spoken about wanting to build products and support companies that reflect the kind of world he hopes his daughters will grow up in.That thinking was part of the reason he established his venture firm, Seven Seven Six, in 2020. In the podcast interview, he explained that becoming a father had made him think more carefully about the professional decisions he was making and the values those decisions represented. He wanted to be able to explain his work to his daughter as she grew older and show her that he had tried to build businesses he could be proud of.His interest in AI also extends beyond family life. He discussed how the technology could help online communities, including by taking some of the repetitive work away from volunteer moderators. He believes AI agents could handle tasks such as identifying spam, leaving community leaders with more time for activities that involve organising people and building relationships.He also spoke about possible uses in sport, where AI could help with player development, scouting and safety, particularly in areas such as women's sport that have historically received less investment.
Article Summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian wants his daughter to explore big questions with AI. He says he wants Olympia to work with AI every day, treating it as a tool for asking questions, exploring ideas and developing her creativity. Ohanian said watching her converse with the system helped him recognise that his own preference for typing was shaped by older experiences with speech-to-text.

Article Title: Dreams bought on credit, lives lost to debt: The human cost of borrowing
Article Text:
With police probing the allegations and the role of lenders and recovery agents, the cases have brought the human cost of debt distress into sharp focus (AI image used for representational purpose)

How loan recovery pressure is pushing borrowers to edge

A Family’s Final Hours: Mounting Loans, Crushing Interest And A Child’s Death

The dark side of loans

A Truck Loan, 2 Missed EMIs, Midnight Calls That Wouldn't Stop And A Death

A Debt They Couldn't Escape, Demands That Wouldn't Stop

Recovery Team Arrives To Take House; Borrower Shoots Himself

When A Friend’s Unpaid Loan Became Her Burden, She Died By Suicide

Mental Harassment Over One Missed EMI Drives Man To Suicide

A Home Loan, A Dream Move And A Life Cut Short Before The First EMI

A Farmer's Death, His Wife's Complaint And 4 Financial Institutions In The Dock





A new home, a struggling business, a medical emergency — loans often promise a fresh start when money falls short.But what begins as a helping hand can sometimes turn into an unbearable burden. For some borrowers, the struggle to repay has spiralled into a relentless cycle of mounting dues, repeated recovery calls and mental distress.From high-interest private loans and missed EMIs to home loans and digital lending platforms, the cases span different forms of borrowing but raise a common concern: the human cost of debt when repayment pressure becomes overwhelming.In a series of tragic incidents, borrowers have died by suicide after allegedly facing pressure over unpaid loans, while financial distress has claimed multiple lives within families.In Pimpri Chinchwad near Pune, alleged harassment by moneylenders over unpaid dues ended in the death of a woman and her 10-year-old son, while her husband survived a suicide attempt and was arrested for the child's murder.The incident took place at the family's 12th-floor flat in Sonawane Vasti, Chikhali. Police said the 45-year-old pharmacy store owner and his 36-year-old wife had been facing constant pressure from moneylenders over loans taken at high monthly interest rates.The woman's brother in Thane alerted police after receiving a message from his sister containing a suicide note.When she stopped responding, police broke into the locked flat and found the couple hanging from a ceiling fan using sarees. Their son was lying motionless on the bed.The husband was breathing and was rushed to hospital, while his wife and son were declared dead.Initially, he told police that the family had decided to end their lives because of harassment by moneylenders. However, a postmortem examination found that the boy had died of asphyxia.Police said the man later admitted to throttling his son after giving him sleeping pills. He and his wife had also consumed sleeping pills before attempting suicide, according to the investigation.Police arrested three moneylenders on charges including abetment and illegal money lending. A separate murder case was registered against the surviving husband.Preliminary investigations found that the family had borrowed money over several years to support its pharmacy business but had failed to repay the dues.In Mumbai's Kandivli East, 27-year-old Suraj Jaiswal allegedly died by suicide hours after a finance company recovery agent took his truck documents following two missed loan instalments.Jaiswal had taken a loan of Rs 15 lakh for a commercial vehicle and had paid three instalments of Rs 32,000 each before missing the next two. His elder brother, Sunil, who was a guarantor, told TOI that recovery agent Vijay Ohal had repeatedly called the family, including late at night.Sunil said he had told the agent to take the truck because his brother was unable to make the payments. The agent collected the vehicle documents, but the calls allegedly continued.Jaiswal had been discharged from hospital about 20 days earlier after undergoing hernia surgery. His family said he had been dealing with health issues and had stopped stepping out after the operation.He was found hanging from a ceiling fan at his home. No suicide note was recovered. Kurar village police registered a case of abetment to suicide against the recovery agent and are investigating the allegations.In Bijnor's Tandhera village, a family of four allegedly consumed poison amid financial distress and harassment by loan recovery agents. Two members died, while the other two were left critically ill.Pukhraj Prajapati, 52, his wife Rameshia, 50, and their daughters Sheetu, 19, and Anita, 17, were rushed to hospital after the incident. Rameshia and Anita died during treatment, while Pukhraj and Sheetu were referred to Meerut Medical College in critical condition.According to police, the family had borrowed more than Rs 6 lakh and was under severe financial stress. Villagers said Pukhraj, who worked as a labourer, had been struggling to repay the growing amount.Police investigations pointed to financial strain and persistent harassment by creditors. Villagers said the family had tried to find ways to repay the loans, but the demands for money continued.Bijnor SP Abhishek Jha said the family had been under considerable stress over the unpaid debt.In Indore, a 55-year-old co-operative bank employee died by suicide as a bank recovery team arrived to take possession of his mortgaged property over unpaid dues on a Rs 2.5 crore loan.Hemant Brahmvanshi shot himself with his licensed double-barrel rifle at his home in Scheme No 74. The bank's recovery team had arrived to evacuate the property after 18 months of unpaid instalments.While bank officials were on the first floor handling paperwork and legal formalities, Brahmvanshi was alone in a room on the ground floor. He shot himself in the head, police said.According to police, he had been struggling with depression amid mounting debt and had received several notices from the bank but had not responded.His eldest son confirmed that his father was undergoing medical treatment for depression. Police seized the firearm, sent the body for postmortem and began recording statements of family members and the recovery team.In Hyderabad, 26-year-old Roja Ramani, an accountant at a private hospital, allegedly died by suicide by jumping into Durgam Cheruvu. Police said she had been under pressure to repay a hand loan taken at a friend's request.According to preliminary investigations, Ramani had borrowed the money for her friend, who subsequently failed to repay it. The lender then allegedly began pressuring her to clear the dues.Madhapur police received information from locals around 11am that a woman had jumped into the lake. Police, with the help of HYDRAA personnel, retrieved the body and sent it for postmortem.Her family had lodged a missing-person complaint at Nagole police station later that night. Police identified her as Ramani and suspected that financial stress had led to her death.In Gujarat, a 36-year-old delivery executive allegedly died by suicide after facing repeated calls from recovery agents over a missed home loan instalment.The man had taken a mortgage loan against his family's house in Chandlodia and had been regularly paying the EMIs before missing an instalment.His family alleged that recovery agents repeatedly called him and mentally harassed him over the pending payment.He left home after returning from work and did not come back. His wife called him around 2.30am, and he said he was outside and would return soon. When he remained unreachable, the family lodged a missing-person complaint.His electric scooter was later found abandoned near the Narmada canal at Jamiyatpura. A handwritten note recovered from it allegedly blamed loan agents for harassment and named two recovery agents, Sahil Rabari and Baldev Maldhari.His body was recovered from the canal near Sherisa village. Following a complaint by his wife, Adalaj police registered an abetment-to-suicide case against the two agents.In Jaipur's Mahesh Nagar, 35-year-old Manisha allegedly died by suicide days after her family bought a house with a Rs 44 lakh home loan.Her family said she had been under severe stress over the repayment, even though the first EMI was yet to be deducted.Manisha lived with her husband, Om Prakash, and their two sons.The family had recently purchased an 86-square-yard house in Hathoj for around Rs 49 lakh. The property was registered eight days before the incident, and the family planned to move after Dev Uthani Ekadashi.After having tea with her husband and children, Manisha asked the children to play outside and locked herself inside a room. Her husband returned after going to get his phone repaired and found the door locked. He broke it open and found her hanging from a saree.Om Prakash told police that his wife had been constantly worried about repaying the home loan. The family had been looking forward to moving into their new house, he said, but the plans ended in tragedy.In Maharashtra's Latur district, police registered a case against officials and employees of four financial institutions over the alleged abetment to suicide of 26-year-old farmer Dattatraya Kumbhar.His wife, Savita, alleged that her husband had faced repeated calls and mental harassment over loan repayments.The complaint also stated that calls demanding money allegedly continued even after his death, despite callers being informed that he had died.Police are identifying employees who contacted Kumbhar before and after his death and examining the role of officials linked to the four institutions. The case was registered under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.Latur SP Amol Tambe said people in urgent need of loans often fall prey to private moneylenders, microfinance companies and online lending applications that charge high interest. He said recovery agents sometimes go to extreme lengths even when instalments are delayed.An Economic Offences Wing officer said complaints had raised concerns about transparency in digital lending, loan closure records and recovery methods.Across these cases, the circumstances and nature of the loans differed. But the investigations point to a recurring concern: borrowers and their families allegedly facing intense pressure when repayments fall behind. With police probing the allegations and the role of lenders and recovery agents, the cases have brought the human cost of debt distress into sharp focus.
Article Summary: In a series of tragic incidents, borrowers have died by suicide after allegedly facing pressure over unpaid loans. In Pimpri Chinchwad near Pune, alleged harassment by moneylenders over unpaid dues ended in the death of a woman and her 10-year-old son. Her husband survived a suicide attempt and was arrested for the child's murder. In Bijhera village, a family of four allegedly consumed poison amid financial harassment by loan agents.
